slides.title: What you will be able to do
objectives: Differentiate a procurement plan from a project plan by scope and purpose
Identify the 8 components of a procurement plan and their role
Select the appropriate contract type given project constraints

slides.title: You already use a project plan
body: Before we talk about procurement plans, let's anchor to something familiar.
- A project plan covers scope, timeline, resources, and deliverables
- It answers: what are we building, and when?
- Every PM creates one — it's the backbone of project execution

slides.title: What is a procurement plan

media.placeholder: Diagram: procurement plan as a parallel document feeding into the project plan

bullets: Defines how purchases will be managed across the project
Covers vendor selection, contract type, and delivery timing
Lives alongside the project plan — not inside it

slides.title: Project plan vs procurement plan
body: Two documents, two questions, one project.
- Project plan asks: WHAT are we building and WHEN?
- Procurement plan asks: HOW do we buy and FROM WHOM?
- Project plan owns scope and schedule — procurement plan owns commercial strategy

slides.title: Three phases of a procurement plan
body: Before we explore all eight components, here's how they organize.
- Define — what to buy (objectives, scope, method)
- Execute — how to buy (contract type, evaluation, risk)
- Govern — who decides (schedule, governance, approvals)

slides.title: Contract type
body: - Fixed-price: risk sits with the vendor, less flexibility for changes
- Time-and-materials: flexibility for the buyer, risk on cost overruns
- Hybrid (capped T&M): shared risk, caps protect the buyer
slides.key_message: Contract type is the single biggest risk-allocation lever in the plan.

slides.title: Evaluation approach
body: - Technical merit: does the solution meet requirements?
- Price competitiveness: is the cost reasonable for the market?
- Risk profile: what could go wrong with this vendor?
- Past performance: has this vendor delivered similar work?
slides.key_message: Weight criteria before you see proposals — not after.

slides.title: Governance and approvals
body: - Define approval authority levels (who signs what value)
- Establish the evaluation panel composition
- Set escalation path for disputes and variations
slides.key_message: Clear governance prevents the 'who approved this?' conversation six months in.

slides.title: Procurement method
body: - Open tender: maximum competition, higher admin effort
- Restricted tender: pre-qualified shortlist, faster
- Direct appointment: speed, but must justify sole-source
slides.key_message: Match the method to the market — don't default to open tender for every package.

slides.title: Objectives and criteria
body: - Clear measurable targets aligned to sponsor expectations
- Evaluation criteria weighted by strategic priority
- Acceptance thresholds agreed with the steering group
slides.key_message: Tie every criterion back to a sponsor-owned success measure.

slides.title: Risk and contingency
body: - Identify procurement-specific risks (vendor insolvency, supply chain disruption)
- Assign risk to the party best positioned to manage it
- Build contingency into timeline and budget — not just cost
slides.key_message: Risk allocation happens in the contract — if it's not written down, you own it.

slides.title: Schedule and milestones
body: - Map procurement timeline to project critical path
- Build in lead times for tender, evaluation, and mobilization
- Identify dependencies between packages
slides.key_message: Procurement delay is the #1 cause of project schedule slip in complex programs.

slides.title: Scope and packaging
body: - Decide single-package vs multi-package procurement
- Balance integration risk against vendor leverage
- Map each package to a delivery milestone
slides.key_message: Packaging is your first risk allocation decision — get it right before vendors are involved.

slides.title: Knowledge check
slides.stem: You're managing a construction project with a well-defined scope, a fixed deadline, and an experienced vendor pool. Which contract type best fits this situation?
options: Time-and-materials — maximum flexibility for scope changes
Fixed-price — risk transferred to vendor, scope is locked
Capped T&M — shared risk with a cost ceiling
Cost-plus — vendor reimbursed for all costs plus a fee
slides.feedback_correct: Fixed-price is the right choice. The scope is well-defined and the deadline is fixed — scope changes are unlikely, so transferring delivery risk to the vendor makes sense.
slides.feedback_incorrect: With a well-defined scope and fixed deadline, fixed-price is the strongest fit. T&M gives flexibility you don't need here, and cost-plus removes the vendor's incentive to control costs.

slides.title: Key takeaways
takeaways: A procurement plan answers 'how will we buy?' — distinct from the project plan's 'what and when?'
Eight components group into three phases: Define, Execute, Govern
Contract type is the biggest risk-allocation lever — match it to scope certainty and timeline pressure
